Nobody knows where the market opens Monday. You don't need to. What you DO need is a plan for whatever happens.

Mark the levels on the names you trade. Check the calendar (this week has bank earnings, CPI and options expiration). Decide the most you're willing to lose this week, and write it down before the first trade.

What does your Sunday prep look like? 👇

posts.caption:
Every trade costs money before it makes any.

Spreads, commissions and fees come out on every round trip, win or lose. They feel tiny one trade at a time. They are NOT tiny over a year.

5 trades a day at $5 per round trip = $6,300 a year.
20 trades a day at $10 per round trip = $50,400 a year.

That's before a single losing trade. Your strategy has to beat that number first just to break even.

The math: trades a day x cost per round trip x 252 trading days. Before taxes.

How many trades do you make a day? Be honest 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.
posts.comment: Spreads and fees are the one loss you're guaranteed. Your edge has to beat them first.

The traders who last aren't the ones who trade the most. They're the ones who can sit through 10 "almost" setups and only pull the trigger on the one that actually fits the plan.

Cash is a position too.

posts.caption:
Calls on Friday. Puts on Saturday. Today: the COVERED CALL. Save this. 📌

You own 100 shares at $100 and sell the $105 call for $2.00. You collect $200 today, no matter what happens next.

At expiration:
→ Stock falls to $90: you lose $800 instead of $1,000 (the premium cushions it)
→ Stock stays at $100: you keep the $200
→ Stock at $105 or higher: you make $700, and that's the max. Your shares can get called away at $105

The trade-off is simple: you get paid now, you give up the big upside, and you still own the downside.

What do you want next: cash-secured puts or spreads? 👇

Hypothetical example, before commissions. Educational only, not financial advice.
posts.comment: A covered call doesn't remove the stock's downside. It only cushions it by the premium.

posts.caption:
Holding a short-dated option and "hoping" is how time decay wins. 🫠

Every day you wait, the option loses a little value. And it's not a straight line: the last few days melt the FASTEST.

That's why so many options go from "down a little" to "worth nothing" in the final week.

Simple fix: decide your exit BEFORE you enter. A profit target, a stop, and a date you'll get out by no matter what.

Ever watched one melt to zero? 👇
posts.comment: Hope is not an exit strategy. Especially with options.

posts.caption:
Would you rather... A or B? 👇

A: Catch the exact bottom once a year, but trade with no rules the rest of the time.
B: Never lose more than 1% on any trade, but never catch a bottom.

Most traders dream about A. It makes the best screenshot.

But the traders still around 10 years later usually live by B. One perfect trade can't fix a hundred careless ones, and a 1% max loss means no single trade can ever knock you out.

A or B? Tell me WHY.
posts.comment: Bottoms make great screenshots. Risk rules make careers.

A missed trade costs $0. A chased trade can cost a lot.

The market makes new setups every single day. You don't need the one that already left.

posts.caption:
Position size is the one decision you control on EVERY trade.

The 1% rule: if your stop gets hit, you lose 1% of your account. Nothing more.

The math: shares = (account x 1%) / (entry price - stop price).

$25,000 account, stop $2 below your entry: 125 shares max.
Same account, stop $5 below: 50 shares.
$10,000 account, $1 stop: 100 shares.

Notice the stop decides the size, not your confidence. A wider stop means fewer shares.

One warning: a stock can gap past your stop overnight, so the real loss can be bigger.

What % do you risk per trade? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.

posts.caption:
That gap is the bid-ask spread, and you pay it every time you trade.

Buy at the $1.10 ask, and if you had to sell right away, you'd only get the $0.90 bid. That's an 18% loss before the stock even moves.

Wide spreads usually show up in options with low volume and low open interest.

How to protect yourself:
→ Check volume and open interest before you trade
→ Use limit orders, not market orders
→ Start near the middle of the spread instead of paying the ask

Do you check the spread before you buy? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.
posts.comment: A tight spread is a free edge. A wide one is a hidden fee.

The lesson isn't "never trade." It's that every trade needs a real reason, because every trade has a real cost.

Do you overtrade? Be honest 👇

posts.caption:
Implied volatility isn't just a number on your options chain. It's the market's estimate of how far a stock could move.

The math: expected move = price x IV x square root of (days / 365). That's a one standard deviation move, which the stock stays inside about 68% of the time.

On a $100 stock:
→ 20% IV: about ±$1.05 a day, ±$5.73 a month
→ 40% IV: about ±$2.09 a day, ±$11.47 a month
→ 80% IV: about ±$4.19 a day, ±$22.94 a month

Why it matters: if you buy an option, the stock usually has to move MORE than the market already expects for you to win. High IV means you're paying for a big move up front.

Do you check IV before you buy? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.

A stop is a decision you made when you were calm. Moving it is a decision you're making when you're scared. Trust the calm version of you.

Before you chase a move this morning, check one thing: is volume higher than normal? If not, be careful.

posts.caption:
Calls, puts, covered calls... today: the CASH-SECURED PUT. Save this. 📌

The stock is at $100. You sell 1 put with a $95 strike for $2.00 and collect $200 today. You set aside $9,500 in cash in case you have to buy 100 shares at $95.

At expiration:
→ Stock stays above $95: the put expires and you keep the $200
→ Stock falls below $95: you buy 100 shares at $95, but your real cost is $93 because of the premium
→ Stock drops to $85: you're down $800 on paper

It's a way to get paid while you wait to buy a stock you already want. The catch: if the stock drops hard, you still own it all the way down.

Only sell puts on stocks you'd be happy to own. Next in the series: spreads?

Hypothetical example, before commissions. Educational only, not financial advice.

posts.caption:

The first time you move a stop, nothing bad happens. The stock comes back. You feel smart.

So you do it again. And the market eventually finds the one time it doesn't come back.

Rule worth tattooing on your monitor: stops only move in ONE direction, toward locking in profit. Never further away from your entry.

posts.caption:

The catch with A: it's a job. Some months it pays more. Some months it pays nothing, or less than nothing.

One buys your time back. The other trades your time for money. A or B, and why?

Educational only, not financial advice.

posts.caption:

A loss that teaches you something is part of the process. A loss you repeat three times is just a habit you haven't faced yet.

After every losing trade, write down three things: what happened, what you felt, and which rule you broke (if any). It takes two minutes.

Read it back once a week. The pattern will jump out at you.

posts.caption:
This is the part of selling options nobody explains until it happens to you.

Most stock options in the U.S. are American-style: the buyer can exercise any time before expiration. If you sold that option, you can be ASSIGNED early.

Sold a covered call? Your shares can get called away. Sold a put? You can be handed 100 shares per contract.
Early assignment is most likely when an option is deep in the money, or right before a dividend for calls.

Index options like SPX are different: they're European-style and cash-settled, so no early assignment.

Trading desks give every trader a daily loss limit. Most people trading from home never set one.

Why it matters: three bad days in a row costs you 6%. Annoying, but fixable. One day of revenge trading can cost 20%, and a 20% loss needs a +25% gain just to get back to even.

posts.caption:
Delta tells you more than how fast an option moves. It's also a rough probability.

Rule of thumb: an option's delta is about its chance of finishing in the money. Its chance of TOUCHING the strike before expiration is about double that.

Example: you sell a 0.20 delta put.
→ About a 20% chance it finishes in the money
→ About a 40% chance the stock trades through your strike at some point before expiration

That's why option sellers get tested far more often than they expect. Your strike getting hit is not rare. Plan for it before you sell.

These are model approximations, not guarantees. Big news can blow right through them.

Do you check delta before you pick a strike? 👇

Educational only, not financial advice.

Calls, puts, covered calls, cash-secured puts... today: the BULL CALL SPREAD. Save this. 📌

The stock is at $100. You buy the $100 call for $4.00 and sell the $110 call for $1.50. Your net cost is $250, and that's the most you can lose.

At expiration:
→ Below $100: you lose the $250
→ At $102.50: break-even
→ At $110 or higher: you make the max, $750

The trade-off: you give up everything above $110 to cut your cost from $400 to $250. A smaller bet with a clear max loss and a clear max win.

This is the options mistake that costs money without anyone noticing.

Example: the stock is at $110. Your $100 call trades at $12.00 with weeks left.

→ Exercise: you buy the stock at $100 when it's worth $110. That's $1,000 of value per contract.
→ Sell the call: you collect $1,200.

The $200 difference is time value, and exercising early throws it away.

Exceptions exist, like deep in-the-money calls right before a dividend, or contracts with very wide bid-ask spreads. Most of the time, selling to close wins.

My wife and I have a 20-minute money talk every Sunday night. It's the most boring part of our week. It's also saved us a LOT of arguments.

We don't do spreadsheets from hell. We go through 4 things:
→ What came in this week
→ What went out (and anything that surprised us)
→ What's coming up (birthdays, car stuff, school things)
→ One thing we're working toward

That's it. No judgment, no "why did you buy that." Just information.

Here's what I've noticed: most money fights aren't really about money. They're about surprises. When you both know what's going on, there's nothing to fight about.
